title: mindthegap
text:
Overview
An R package for Agent Based Modelling (ABM) of whole blood donors donating at stochastic intervals.

title: mindthegap
text:
Themes / Analytical methods
R package, OOP with R6 classes, coupled ordinary differential equations for System Dynamics, Agent Based Modelling, Monte Carlo Methods, Shiny app, composite metric, Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis

title: mindthegap
text:
Business Problem
European law allows more frequent donation than NHSBT currently allows in England, so would it be a good idea to let people donate more frequently?

Academic aim
On reducing the minimum allowed interval between successive blood donations, does any increase in blood supply significantly outweigh any deterioration of body iron health in donors?

title: mindthegap
text:
Scoping and planning



Extract from a presentation on the project


After interviewing clinical stakeholders, I recognised the aim of the model should be to simulate a cohort of blood donors and their instances of successful blood donations over a fixed time period. The distribution of the number of donations made by each simulated donor, and the intervals between them, should be expected to be a function of: * The minimum interval * The donor’s individual preferred interval between donations * The time required for the donor’s blood iron levels to replenish sufficiently to pass the Hb test
A reduction in the minimum interval is expected to increase the total number of donations from donors over a fixed period of time, accompanied by an increase in the frequency and severity of adverse effects on donors’ body iron health. The model should allow the practitioner to vary, as an input parameter, the minimum allowed donation interval, and should return a quantified set of donor outcomes, pertaining to blood supply and donor body iron health.
Model methodology and outputs should be transparent, explicit, and granular enough for a practitioner to draw quantitative, parameterised insights and statistical expectations surrounding the tradeoff between blood supply and donor body iron health. Simultaneously, model outputs should be accessible and practical enough to lend themselves to a solving a cost-benefit analysis rooted in that trade-off, and to reasonably inform a recommendation for an operational intervention or policy.

title: mindthegap
text:
Assumptions
Key assumptions relate to:

A sequential process flow for a donor choosing to donate blood through to the physical donation
Distributional assumptions governing how long after their last donation a donor will choose to donate
The dynamics of iron in the human body (especially replenishment) that govern whether a donor passes the pre-donation Haemoglobin test

title: mindthegap
text:
Technical choices

I recognised the suitability of Agent-Based Modelling (ABM), given the idiosyncratic and behavioural nature of donors choosing to donate. A good model would require fine control over a range of different parameters and variables.



Agent Based Model overview



Overview of ABM paradigm




ABM example



Example application of ABM




Example parameters and variables



Extract from presentation on project





I decided to develop an R package to allow for fine control over testing different scenarios under different parameters. The donors, with their preferences, variabiality, and complex iron dynamics, warranted the use of an Object Oriented Programming approach using R6 Classes. Donor objects are instantiated, equipped with their own stochastic characteristics and behaviour, and iron replenishment mechanics.
I used a Monte Carlo Method with hierarchical sampling to effectively and efficiently simulate a highly stochastic system of a donor’s donation activity.
I used a composite metric of a linear combination of donations and permanent deferrals (after three failed pre-donation Haemoglobin tests, donors cannot return)
I included observables relating to “wasted slots” and donor burnout, for scope to extend the composite metric

title: Capacity Network Design
text:
Overview
A greedy algorithm to explore interactions between the competing operational objectives in deciding how blood donation collection appointments (slots) should be distributed geographically.

title: Capacity Network Design
text:
Themes / Analytical methods
R, Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis, Computational statistics/Numerical methods, leaflet choropleth geo-mapping, conveying abstract concepts to decision-makers

title: Capacity Network Design
text:
Business Problem

Problem statement
The organisation’s current operational setup for blood donation collection is not optimised. Appointments (slots) are not optimally distributed in either a spatial or temporal sense i.e. people who are willing and able to donate blood cannot always find a slot near them, at a suitable time. What would the collection capacity network looked like if we rebuilt it from scratch in the optimal way?


Academic Aim
A numerical method by way of a greedy algorithm that, given a set of organisational objectives along with relative weights or priorities, allocates a given number of appointments geographically so as to maximise the likelihood of meeting those objectives.

title: Capacity Network Design
text:
Scoping and planning

I decided to consider an optimisation problem with respect to only the spatial distributiion of slots, as a first step. I recognised that the temporal aspect could be dealt with independently, because I had no reason to believe that the optimal temporal distribution should be significantly different between geographical areas - as such the problem could be reduced to two independent optimisation problems, of which I would tackle the spatial one in the first instance.
I recognised this as an application for Multi-Criterion Decision Analysis (MCDA), especially considering the difficulty of expressing different organisational objectives in comparable terms e.g. collecting enough blood from Black African and Black Caribbean donors, and minimising the distance collected blood needs to travel to manufacturing sites

title: Capacity Network Design
text:
Technical choices

I recognised that the optimal solution would be a function of the ordering or weighting of the competing orgnisational objectives, and so chose to use a computational approach of an algorithm that incrementally added capacity to the next-best location at each step (greedy) by using an objective function that was a weighted average of “monetised” or otherwise quantified organisational objectives
I decided that a solution that conveyed the above mechanic, that the weighting/priority strongly determined the optimum, was more important to convey to decision-makers than converging on a contrived or otherwise arbitrary “objective” optimum. As such, I felt justified in using an approach that can sometimes miss the global optimum.
The computational approach with the weighted objective function also allowed me to

demonstrate with fine control how tweaking or varying the weighted shifted the optimum in the direction of different extremes, to non-technical decision makers
compute and compare different scenarios side by side

As a proof of concept (POC) I developed a Shiny app with inputs for parameters to demonstrate the reduction of the problem down to the weighted objectives

title: Intuitive Hypothesis Tests
text:
Overview
An interactive Shiny app with dynamic visualisations to convey the intuition behind a hypothesis test.

title: Intuitive Hypothesis Tests
text:
Themes / Analytical methods
R, Shiny, reactivity, widgets, presenting complex technical concepts accessibly, presenting to different audiences simultaneously

title: Intuitive Hypothesis Tests
text:
Business Problem
I’m passionate about promoting data literacy and empowering the stakeholders I work with to understand the methods in the analysis I provide, rather than just the recommendation. This was an informal “Lunch and Learn” talk I delivered to a mix of technical and non-technical people. I wanted to deliver a session that:

unlocked the intuition behind hypothesis testing, that non-technical people didn’t know they already had
for people who were familiar with hypothesis testing in a syntactical/“textbook” way, provide and showcase a sandbox of mechanics that they could play with independently, to make the principles “click”

title: Intuitive Hypothesis Tests
text:
Scoping and planning
I recognised that if this were to be effective:

it would need to take a very different approach to a textbook providing formulae for test statistics and tables for critical values. Also, the delivery and format would need to be engaging
it would need to draw on intuition and experience that people already have. This would serve to build confidence in the attendees as we explored technical material, and prevent the talk from feeling like an academic exercise or thought-experiment.
the scope of the product would need to be such that people could not only benefit from attending my talk, but also could benefit further from playing around with the app, if they chose to.

title: Intuitive Hypothesis Tests
text:
Technical choices
Based on my Scoping and Planning reflections:

I decided to create and publish an open-source interactive Shiny app, which would allow me to talk through instructive examples, and allow keener attendees to play with the app in their own time
I decided to start my presentation with some examples of hypothesis tests that people are likely to have conducted “qualitatively” in their day to day life e.g. Wondering whether you’ve been incorrectly served a Diet Coke (Alternative hypothesis) means you had an expectation of a certain taste from a regular Coke (Null hypothesis), and the taste is so different to that expectation (test statistic) that it feels too unlikely (p value) that it is a regular Coke. This also provided a good opportunity to make technical terms stick, and showing that people already understand the concept even if they didn’t know the jargon.
I transitioned from qualitative examples to the classic example of a series of fair coin tosses. Next, to a biased coin, and then with some relabelling of the biased coin, to a toy example from genomics - testing whether a “test” string of bases is a mutation of a reference string or a different string entirely, based on an independent probability of mutation (the bias of the coin). This provided a seamless but significant transition from the qualitative Coke example to a good setting for a quantitative treatment of the subject matter: If there were “few” positions different between the test and reference strings (the Hamming Distance), we wouldn’t believe the test string is anything other than a mutation of the reference string - if there were a large Hamming Distance, we would be led to stop believing the test string is simply a mutation of the reference string. Genomics felt like a good level of “close to home”, given the donor-recipient matching necessary for blood donation that my organisation is concerned with.
From here, I continued in an incremental fashion to keep people confident and engaged:

Using a dynamic graph, I talked through the Probabilty Mass Function (PMF) for the Hamming Distance, and demonstrating how it smoothly and intuitively changed as you vary the length of the string (n) and the independent probability of mutation (p).
From here it was simple to explain that we add the bars to get the cumulative PMF.
The next graph added an (arbitrary) line at the 95% mark to define “extreme” outcomes in that that pobserving an outcome at least as extreme was only 5% if they Null were true.

I explained that the app was publicly available and provided the URL and suggested playing around by varying (n, p) and observing the “wave” that moved and changed which outcomes started to become “significant”, explaining this is the essence of critical values. This kept the Lunch and Learn to a manageable length while suggesting further avenues to explore for the keener attendees.
From experience, hypothesis testing in an academic usually starts from the Normal distribution. I chose instead to use the Binomial distribution (for number of Heads / Hamming Distance) because this felt like the distribution that people already have the most intuition for. I did wonder whether the discreteness PMFs might be less digestible (at least for some more “jagged” combinations of (n, p)) than a continuous Probability Distribution Function, but actually I concluded that not needing to go into probability density was an advantage.

title: Intuitive Hypothesis Tests
text:
Validation and Impact
These kinds of presentations can be harder to get constructive feedback from, because people are usually grateful for the effort that went into it. As such, I try to monitor from the nature of and depth questions and remarks whether the material has hit home. Again, fairly qualitatively, I try to see whether ideas I discuss then present in stakeholders’ thoughts when we plan work together. While I can’t directly attribute it to the Lunch and Leanr, I was pleased to hear an attendee later remark, in a meeting to discuss a campaign evaluation, that we would need a control group because we would need to know what would have happened without the marketing intervention to form the initial expectation in the first place.

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
text:
Overview
A quarto book journalling my journey of playing Fantasy Premier League (FPL) using statistics and the FPL API and no football knowledge.

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
text:
Themes / Analytical methods
Effective and deliberate scoping and planning, project management “discipline”, Python, Quarto, API endpoints, time series analysis, designing heuristic metrics

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
text:
Business Problem
During data science or operational work, particularly more complex or unstructured work, I often notice the temptation or inclination to consider applying manual overrides to my methodology or scope - perhaps to account for an edge case or an extra variable that becomes apparent later. While this comes from a place of quality or rigour, and can be the best thing to do if done properly/iteratively, I recognise that actually if the override/overlay/correction that occurs to me is truly value-adding, then that means my original scoping and planning could have been better i.e. scoping and planning should at the outset aim to sufficiently but minimally capture all that is necessary and useful in designing a good solution to a problem.
This project occurred to me as a useful exercise in discipline of devising a strategy to solve a problem (scoring as many points as possible in FPL) knowing that my domain knowledge is significantly limited, choosing a boundary of information to be “in scope” as a heuristic solution to that limitation, and then not intervening or overriding when I inevitably encounter information out of the scope. I envisaged, and experiencing, a huge amount of advice and suggestions from friends who do have a “football IQ”, and the idea is for me to have spent enough time prior to Gameweek 1 planning a strategy I am happy with and confident in, with the information I choose to use, so that I don’t then throughout the season succumb to the temptation to bolt on extra bits of strategy as I go along. How many points I score is actually do is in many ways less important to me than how well I managed the scope creep.

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
text:
Scoping and planning
The chapter of my Quarto book linked below explores the scope I set out for myself before looking at any data or choosing any players. The chapter is structured by way of tenuous football references.
https://janarthduraisingham.github.io/fpl/intro.html

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
text:
Technical choices

Approaching the problem
I recognised that the problem could be reduced into two different, but interacting, sub-problems:

Before Gameweek 1, I need to choose an initial squad that is likely to score well
Each week, I need to use my transfers to sell players who are likely to score badly and buy players who are likely to score well



Statistical methodology
While the two sub-problems sound similar, I recognised that I would have significantly different data on which to solve them. I can make weekly transfers using data that was realised the prior weekend, but I had to choose my initial squad based on prior season data relating to months or years ago.

I decided to select my initial squad based on the last two (aggregated) seasons of data

To leave myself with capital to make informed transfers on more current data later in the season, I would prioritise a cheap squad with a high historical points to current price ratio.
More details here: https://janarthduraisingham.github.io/fpl/gw1.html

I decided to select weekly transfers based on recent current season data

I used a heuristic mix of a 4 week Simple Moving Average, and an Exponentially-Weighted Moving Average Crossover to rank and select candidiates to transfer in and out.
More details here, including technical discussion and step-by-step computation: https://janarthduraisingham.github.io/fpl/gw7.html

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
text:
Validation
With 37 transfers over the season and 15 players in the squad, the average number of players holding any one position is less than 3. I recognised that this meant that if choose my initial squad badly, that puts a lot of pressure on the weekly transfers to make up the forgone value and add their own value. For this reason I didn’t want my measure of performance to reflect a combination of my performance of picking a good squad on old data (which was likely to be a worse predictor) and of my performance of making good decisions based on my transfers strategy.
For this reason I decided my main metric of evaluation would be to compare my final points at the end of the season with the points my initial squad would have scored, had I made no transfers over the season. In this way, I’m able to deliberately and specifically evaluate how well my strategy identified good transfers, regardless of how well my initial squad was chosen.
More details here: https://janarthduraisingham.github.io/fpl/intro.html#the-goalposts

title: Fantasy Premier League [Personal, WIP]
section: What I learnt / would improve & Relevance to Senior Data Scientist role
text:
What I learnt / would improve & Relevance to Senior Data Scientist role
This a valuable and rare exercise in that it’s otherwise quite uncommon to undertake a technical task having almost no domain knowledge. I’ve gone into this knowing that with the scope of my strategy, there’s probably quite a low ceiling of performance, which makes implementing the tips and advice I hear from knowledgeable friends more tempting to quietly include - most notably “Captain Haaland”. Processing and acknowledging that temptation and choosing to respect the scope and plan has been a valuable exercise in discipline for me.
It also highlights the importance of including a range of stakeholders upstream and early on, when, as is usual, a low ceiling of performance is not acceptable. Ultimately, practising data science as a non-clinician means projects are likely to include a never-ending horizon of possible depth to explore. A key part of scoping and planning is deciding on a modelling/analytical scope, drawing on perspectives and experiences from a diverse range of colleague and stakeholders to fully explore that scope, and then respect it without succumbing to scope creep.
